sections.title: Original sin

questions.prompt: How does Adam’s sin affect a person before that person has chosen anything?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Humanity shares both a damaged nature and liability to judgment through Adam.

choices.label: B
choices.text: We inherit a wounded condition and mortality. Personal culpability belongs to our own sin.

choices.label: C
choices.text: We enter a world shaped by others’ sin, without inheriting a sinful nature or guilt.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I affirm universal human sinfulness but do not claim to know how Adam’s act is transmitted to us.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: In what sense can Paul say that all sinned in connection with one man?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adam acted as humanity’s appointed representative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Humanity was in some real sense present or participating in Adam.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adam opened the reign of sin and death under which each person comes to sin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adam portrays the universal human turning from God.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: If humanity inherited mortality without individual guilt for Adam’s act, would everyone still need Christ?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. Deliverance from corruption and death is itself a saving work only Christ can accomplish.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes. Universal personal sin also gives everyone capable of personal action a need for forgiveness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both claims belong together in my account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I do not accept the proposed distinction between inherited mortality and liability in Adam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

introduction: Ancestral sin is a term especially common in Eastern Christian discussions of humanity’s inheritance from Adam.
editorialNotes: A historical account of Adam is available in ANT. Here the issue is the connection between Adam’s sin and ours.

furtherStudy.text: Orthodox Church in America, “St. Augustine & Original Sin.” Its account speaks of the “consequences” of sin, “the chief of which is death.”
Westminster Confession, chapter VI, on the fall, guilt, and corruption.

sections.title: Inherited guilt and corruption

questions.prompt: If an infant has done no deliberate wrong, what could “original sin” mean in that infant’s case?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: The infant stands in Adam’s guilt through representation, even without a personal act.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The infant lacks original holiness and needs healing or grace, without bearing personal blame for Adam’s act.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The infant inherits mortality and life in a disordered world, without a transmitted sinful condition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The term should be reserved for personal sin and therefore does not apply to the infant.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: Does forgiveness or removal of original sin remove every inclination toward sin?
questions.displayNote: ↳ After HAM-04, if A or B is selected.

choices.label: A
choices.text: No. The inclination remains and is itself sinful even when resisted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No. The inclination remains, but it becomes personal sin through consent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: God can also cleanse an inherited disposition to sin in a further work of grace.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I would distinguish forgiveness from healing but am unsure how to classify the remaining inclination.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: Does sharing in the effects of wrongdoing necessarily mean sharing the wrongdoer’s guilt?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: No. A person can suffer consequences without being guilty of the act.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Usually no, but a representative relationship can make another’s act judicially count as one’s own.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A community can bear real corporate guilt without every member bearing the same personal culpability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I’m unsure.

editorialNotes: Separate personal blame, a judicial status, and the effects of living under sin and death.

furtherStudy.text: Compendium of the Catechism, questions 75–78, on original sin and its consequences.

sections.title: Total depravity and moral inability

questions.prompt: How far does sin reach into human nature?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: It affects every faculty, including our capacity to turn to God.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It deeply wounds human nature while leaving a natural capacity to begin seeking God.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concerns our actual choices and habits more than any inherited impairment of our faculties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: A person who does not believe in God cares for an enemy at real personal cost. What could you affirm about the act?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is genuinely good toward the neighbor, while lacking what would make it righteous before God in the fullest sense.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can be pleasing to God as an act of love even without the person’s explicit faith.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its goodness is already a sign of grace at work, though I would leave the person’s standing before God open.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I would distinguish degrees of goodness without making the person’s explicit beliefs decisive.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

editorialNotes: “Total” can refer to the reach of sin across human faculties. It does not quantify the cruelty of any individual.

sections.title: Nature and consequences of sin

questions.prompt: Which realities can properly be called sin?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: A deliberate wrongful act.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure to do good that one owes another.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An inward desire contrary to love of God or neighbor, even before deliberate consent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A settled disposition turning a person away from God.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A communal practice or institution that does wrong, even where responsibility is distributed.

choices.label: F
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: Once an unwanted temptation arises, at what point is there personal sin?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: The disordered desire can itself be sinful even when the person resists it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Personal sin begins when the person welcomes or consents to the desire.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The answer depends on whether we mean an involuntary attraction, a cultivated desire, or a deliberate intention.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: Are some sins different in kind in their effect on a believer’s communion with God?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. Certain grave sins can destroy that communion when knowingly and deliberately chosen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sins vary greatly in gravity, but I do not divide them into kinds that retain or destroy saving grace.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent or repudiating sin can break communion, though I would not define the divide by a fixed class of acts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: When someone fails to help a neighbor, which considerations bear on whether the omission is sinful?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes. Love of neighbor can create a real obligation in the circumstances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, when the omission violates an identifiable duty of one’s role or an applicable moral command.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There may be a generous action one could take without its omission necessarily being sin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The answer depends on the person’s knowledge, ability, and competing responsibilities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

editorialNotes: Distinguish temptation, consent, omission, structural wrong, and degrees of sin.

sections.title: Human ability after the Fall

questions.prompt: Before receiving grace that enables a response, can a fallen person take the first step toward saving faith?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: No. God must first give life or enable a response.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person can begin to seek God, but cannot reach saving faith without further grace.

choices.label: C
choices.text: I reject the imagined starting point. God’s enabling presence already reaches every person.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The capacity to answer God belongs to created human nature even after the fall.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

editorialReview.workingBankPrompt: Before any grace that enables a response, can a fallen person take the first step toward saving faith?
editorialReview.reason: The current friend edition has the displayed wording. The working bank retains this earlier formulation.

questions.prompt: If two people hear the same invitation and only one believes, what might account for the difference?
questions.displayNote: ↳ After HAM-12, if A or C is selected.

choices.label: A
choices.text: God gave an effectual grace that brought one person to faith.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both were enabled by grace, and one freely resisted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Their histories, understanding, or circumstances affect how the invitation is received.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The difference is real, but Scripture does not reveal enough to assign a decisive explanation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: How does an enduring habit of sin affect a person’s responsibility?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: It may deepen responsibility when a person has repeatedly chosen and cultivated it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It may diminish responsibility for particular acts by reducing freedom or awareness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both can be true of the same person at different stages or in different respects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Responsibility rests on the act’s moral character regardless of how the habit formed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: I’m unsure.

questions.prompt: When Scripture calls people “dead” in sin, what should the image lead us to affirm?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: A radical inability to come to saving faith unless God first gives life.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alienation from God and bondage to sin, overcome by a grace that can be resisted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A real condition of estrangement, without the image by itself settling the order of grace and response.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I’m unsure.

editorialNotes: Do not treat unaided ability and an ability already restored by grace as the same answer.

furtherStudy.text: Church of the Nazarene, Articles of Faith, V and VII, on sin and prevenient grace.
Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration II, on the will and conversion.

editorialNotes: Enter at any dimension. In guided mode, begin with its opening question, continue through the main questions in the order shown, and insert a follow-up only when its stated answer matches. After the branch, resume with the next main question. A skipped answer or uncertainty opens no conditional branch unless specified.

Choose the closest single answer unless multiple selections are invited. On multiple-response questions, an uncertainty or “none” choice stands alone. Treat unresolved tensions as invitations to clarify.

vocabulary.definition: The study of sin, its origins, its effects, and human responsibility.
The biblical account of humanity’s first disobedience and the resulting condition of life estranged from God.
Humanity’s fallen condition connected to Adam’s sin and present before a person chooses to sin.
vocabulary.expandedNote: Traditions differ over what is inherited. The Westminster Confession speaks of imputed guilt and corrupted nature. The Catholic Catechism calls original sin a condition inherited by Adam’s descendants and distinguishes it from their personal fault. An Eastern Orthodox account emphasizes humanity’s inheritance of death and corruption.

vocabulary.definition: A term used in Eastern Orthodox theology for humanity’s inheritance of death and corruption through Adam’s disobedience.
The Reformed teaching that sin affects every part of human nature and leaves people unable to turn to God in saving faith apart from grace.
vocabulary.expandedNote: “Total” refers to the reach of sin across the person. The doctrine can distinguish ordinary acts of human kindness from the ability to turn to God for salvation. HAM-06 and HAM-07 explore those questions separately.

vocabulary.definition: The inability of fallen people to turn to God in saving faith apart from enabling grace.
In Catholic theology, a sin that destroys charity in the heart when it involves grave matter, full knowledge, and deliberate consent.
In Catholic theology, a sin that wounds charity in the heart while leaving the person’s friendship with God intact.
